title: Advanced Advanced Dungeons & Dragons

jokes.text: I can ask on the street. / Oh, too cool for street insurance? Must be nice.
jokes.setup: The committee discusses needing insurance for the school, a mundane administrative topic.
jokes.punchline: Hickey immediately volunteers to 'ask on the street' as if street insurance is a real thing, then doubles down with wounded pride when questioned.
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold-open Hickey joke. The concept of 'street insurance' is absurd but delivered with total conviction, and the wounded-pride follow-up ('Must be nice') is a great character beat. Only Hickey would have underworld connections for insurance AND feel socially slighted when not taken up on it.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Committee Member
dialogue.line: Yeah, and then we can get some street insurance, maybe pick up some black market health care on the corner.

jokes.text: My sister wants to know what I'm bringing to my grandson's birthday.
jokes.setup: The meeting continues on the insurance topic, an apparent non sequitur.
jokes.punchline: Hickey has completely moved on to a personal family issue with no transition, treating it as equally pressing meeting business.
jokes.explanation: Good economical pivot that establishes the episode's B-plot conflict while being funny purely through the non sequitur delivery. Hickey treating personal family drama as agenda-worthy committee business is a solid character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I have two sons.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I only understand one of them.

jokes.text: I'm sensing an emergency collage situation.
jokes.setup: Hickey has revealed he wasn't invited to his grandson's birthday, clearly distressed.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's instinctive response to emotional pain is to propose a collage, her signature comfort-craft solution.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Shirley line. The word 'emergency' in front of 'collage situation' is doing a lot of heavy lifting — it implies this is a category of crisis she has a protocol for. Pure character-integration comedy; no one else in the ensemble could deliver this.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: My grandson's birthday is coming up.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh! We should make him a collage!

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: A collage?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You know, pictures and memories all put together! It'll be so meaningful!

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I think you mean a college fund.

jokes.text: I wasn't invited. My son had a kid three years ago. I barely get to see him on major holidays.
jokes.setup: Hickey explains the family situation that prompted the non sequitur.
jokes.punchline: The cascade of increasingly sad details — not invited, didn't know for three years, barely sees him even on holidays — delivered in Hickey's flat, matter-of-fact cop voice.
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is tonal — the information is genuinely sad but Hickey's delivery is so clipped and stoic that it becomes funny. The escalating sadness of each detail builds well.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You mean the game?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We're gonna use it to help you.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I know. That's what makes it stupid.

jokes.text: I mean, who in the hell does he think he is? / You saw your son at his wedding. / No, that's Furio, my gay son. Him, I get.
jokes.setup: Someone points out Hickey did see his son at his wedding, suggesting the estrangement isn't total.
jokes.punchline: Hickey clarifies there are TWO sons — the problem son Hank, and Furio, the gay son 'him, I get' — delivered with no self-awareness about how the qualifier sounds.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'That's Furio, my gay son. Him, I get.' is a brilliantly compressed character reveal — it surprises us with a second son, the name 'Furio' is itself funny, and the addendum 'Him, I get' implies Hickey finds the supposedly more difficult category of son easier to understand than his straight one. It subverts expectations about what a gruff cop character would find relatable. Highly quotable, economical, and reveals character depth.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Our last D&D game nearly ended in tragedy.

jokes.text: Hank's a knob, doesn't have any hobbies, interests. All he does is play... What do you call that crap with dungeons and dragons?
jokes.setup: Hickey describes his son Hank critically, building to what his one hobby is.
jokes.punchline: The hobby Hickey can't remember the name of is literally 'Dungeons and Dragons' — the name of the game the study group already plays.
jokes.explanation: The setup works well: Hickey calling D&D 'that crap with dungeons and dragons' while literally not being able to recall the name is funny character comedy. The payoff of the group immediately recognizing it sets up the episode's premise efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, we did what we had to do. Neil needed an intervention.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: He's doing fine now.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, he's... you know, he's out there. Doing his thing. Living his life or whatever.

jokes.text: 'Dungeons and Dragons'? / That's the crap.
jokes.setup: Someone supplies the game's actual name.
jokes.punchline: Hickey's flat confirmation 'That's the crap' — he doesn't elevate his description now that he knows the name.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words that land as a callback button to the previous joke. The deflation of 'That's the crap' vs. the proper noun is funny in its stubborn dismissiveness.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You know what they say about sequels. They're never as good as the original.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not always true.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Name one good sequel.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: The Dark Knight.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Okay, name another one.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Terminator 2.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Those don't count. I'm going to run the best D&D campaign this group has ever seen. Better than my first one. Better than anything any of you could do. You're going down.

jokes.text: Was everyone's takeaway last time that we use 'D&D' to reprogram brains?
jokes.setup: Jeff enthusiastically proposes using D&D again to fix Hickey's family relationship, echoing the Season 4 episode.
jokes.punchline: Abed cuts through the group's optimism with a precise meta-critique of their own narrative logic, questioning the lesson they drew from their last D&D adventure.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed — he's the show's internal critic, and this line punctures the meta-structural impulse that drives the episode while also being a sharp joke about the group's questionable therapeutic interventions. It earns extra points for rewatchers who remember Season 4.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Well, I get to be a character who's powerful and respected, I go on adventures, and nobody can tell me I'm doing it wrong.

jokes.text: Not that we almost caused a suicide? / We prevented one. Fa... bulous Neil felt like a nobody.
jokes.setup: Abed points out the near-tragedy of the last D&D session.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's rationalization stumbles mid-word — he almost says 'Fat Neil' before self-correcting to 'Fabulous Neil' — revealing the group's uncomfortable history.
jokes.explanation: The mid-word stammer 'Fa...bulous Neil' is superb — it's simultaneously a callback joke, a character revelation about Jeff's lingering bad habits, and a dark subversive beat. The audience hears exactly what Jeff almost said. High craft: tiny moment, big comedic and character payoff.

jokes.text: And thanks to us, he's still out there, doing this and that in the background.
jokes.setup: Jeff is making the case that the last D&D session was a success because Neil survived.
jokes.punchline: The best Jeff can say about Neil's post-rescue life is that he's 'doing this and that in the background' — a hilariously low bar for 'we saved his life.'
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-serving rationalization that Neil's value is merely existing 'in the background' is both a great character moment and a darkly funny commentary on the limits of their heroism. 'Doing this and that in the background' is a wonderfully dismissive phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's my son.

jokes.text: Satisfying sequel's difficult. Many geniuses defeated themselves through hubris. Making this a chance to prove I'm better. I'm in!
jokes.setup: The group is debating whether to do another D&D session.
jokes.punchline: Abed frames his participation purely in terms of narrative craft and his own artistic ego — treating the human stakes (Hickey's family) as irrelevant compared to the challenge of writing a better sequel.
jokes.explanation: Abed's meta-awareness here is both funny and character-perfect. He explicitly treats the episode as a sequel and his role as DM as an artistic challenge. The escalating self-aggrandizement ('many geniuses... I'm better') is a great beat. Only Abed could say this.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: The obviously contrived father-son setup

jokes.text: So, Dad... I'm just curious. What is it about 'Dungeons and Dragons' that suddenly leapt out at you at age 60?
jokes.setup: Hickey's son Hank meets his father before the game, ostensibly to reconnect.
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately calls out the transparent manipulation — his father has never shown interest in D&D and suddenly at 60 he's playing? The sarcasm is dry and knowing.
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of the audience's assumption that Hank won't see through the scheme. His dry skepticism establishes him as a foil to his father's bluntness — he's not an idiot. The '60' specification adds comedic specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm Jeff Winger. I'm a lawyer. Well, I was a lawyer. I'm also very handsome and I have a ridiculous amount of charisma.

jokes.text: Dungeons. It'd be the dungeons.
jokes.setup: Hank asks his father what aspect of D&D attracted him. It's a pointed, rhetorical question.
jokes.punchline: Hickey answers with complete sincerity and deadpan literalism — he picked one of the two words in the game's title and committed to it.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Dungeons. It'd be the dungeons.' is exquisitely crafted — four words that do enormous work. Hickey has zero interest in the game, got caught in a transparent lie, and his coping strategy is to pick one word from the name and claim that's what he likes. The pause before 'It'd be the dungeons' implies a split-second of calculation. Perfect character integration, perfect economy. Highly quotable standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Look, I don't have time for fantasy complexity. I've got a color-coded study schedule, three extracurriculars, and I'm pretty sure I'm failing Spanish.

jokes.text: Oh, that's just what I love about role-playing games... is being told exactly what to do.
jokes.setup: Abed gives an elaborate, atmospheric description of the opening scenario with a clear objective.
jokes.punchline: Hank's flat, withering sarcasm reveals he finds the prescribed nature of the adventure condescending — which also reflects his attitude toward his father's forced bonding attempt.
jokes.explanation: Hank's sarcasm works on two levels — it's both a critique of railroad-style D&D adventure design AND a subtext commentary on being pushed into this reunion. The double meaning elevates it above a simple snarky line.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You know what? Fine. From now on, you can all call me... Kevin.

jokes.text: Oh, boy. Joseph Gordon Diehard. Really? Son of Sir Riggs Diehard. / Well, I'm Sir Riggs Diehard, so I guess I'm your dad in the game too.
jokes.setup: Hickey reads his character's name and backstory — it's transparently engineered to replicate his real-life father-son dynamic.
jokes.punchline: Jeff notes the obvious, then Hickey immediately clocks that he got the father role, completing the too-on-the-nose metaphor.
jokes.explanation: Functional joke that exposes the scheme. Jeff's 'Really?' is the audience surrogate, and Hickey quickly catching on is good. The name 'Joseph Gordon Diehard' is itself a bit funny as an obvious contrivance.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, my character name is Dingleberry? Like the thing that gets stuck in your butt hair?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yes, Chang. That's exactly what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: This is the worst day of my life.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, so cool. / Isn't that weird?
jokes.setup: Hickey has clocked the manipulative character assignments; the room is tense.
jokes.punchline: Dean Pelton responds with pure uncritical enthusiasm while Annie is mortified — their completely opposite registers in the same beat.
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat that uses character contrast efficiently. Dean's oblivious enthusiasm vs. Annie's awareness of the awkwardness is a quick, well-timed double reaction.

jokes.text: Oh, boy. Guys, I don't suppose this is some contrived paint-by-numbers adventure that's designed to force an emotional bond between me and my emotionally stunted father, is it?
jokes.setup: The group has been caught out designing a transparently manipulative D&D scenario.
jokes.punchline: Hank calls it out with forensic precision — 'contrived paint-by-numbers,' 'emotionally stunted father' — and his delivery is calm and devastatingly accurate.
jokes.explanation: Good meta-line that also works as a critique of the episode's own premise. 'Paint-by-numbers adventure' is a smart phrase. The specificity of 'emotionally stunted father' as a clinical diagnosis rather than an insult is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm tired of following this predetermined path. I'm going off-road.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: These so-called 'boundaries' are just artificial limitations designed to contain us. Well, not on my watch.

jokes.text: No way, Jose. / What?
jokes.setup: Hank asks if the adventure is a contrived emotional-bonding exercise. Jeff denies it.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response is 'No way, Jose' — an absurdly casual, almost childish denial — and Hank's 'What?' registers the inadequacy of this deflection.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the inadequacy of Jeff's deflection — using a playground-level denial against a pointed adult question. Hank's 'What?' captures the audience's reaction perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This is fun! This is so much fun. We're having fun right now. Fun!

jokes.text: I'm Tristram Steelheart. I'm a holy cleric with a mace and a dumb name.
jokes.setup: Characters are introducing their reshuffled D&D personas.
jokes.punchline: Jeff introduces himself and immediately editorializes that his own character has 'a dumb name' — breaking the fiction before it's even established.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's unwillingness to commit to the fiction even when introducing himself is perfectly in character. The self-deprecating footnote 'and a dumb name' subverts the heroic introduction format efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We're having fun.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Fun?! Ha ha ha! Yes! Fun! I love fun! Ha ha ha ha! *forced laughter intensifies* This is me having fun! Isn't this fun, everyone? I'm having so much fun right now! Ha ha ha! *manic grin* Fun fun fun fun FUN!

jokes.text: I'm Tiny Nuggins, a thief, and the rest is gibberish.
jokes.setup: Characters are introducing their D&D personas with their stats and class.
jokes.punchline: Shirley gives her name and class then dismisses all subsequent character detail as 'gibberish' — she's playing along but on her own terms.
jokes.explanation: 'The rest is gibberish' is excellent economy. Shirley participating minimally while vocally relegating the game mechanics to nonsense is a great character beat. The name 'Tiny Nuggins' on Shirley is itself visual-comedy adjacent.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I cast a spell to make myself too heavy to carry.

dialogue.speaker: Dungeon Master
dialogue.line: You're not a wizard.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Then I'm a rogue. I use my rogue skills to escape.

dialogue.speaker: Dungeon Master
dialogue.line: You fail. They carry you away.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I attack them with my sword!

dialogue.speaker: Dungeon Master
dialogue.line: Roll for it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I got a twenty!

dialogue.speaker: Dungeon Master
dialogue.line: You hit one of them. Roll damage.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Twelve damage. Now I'm actually trying to kill them.

jokes.text: Greetings, I am Fibrosis the Ranger.
jokes.setup: Characters are naming their D&D personas.
jokes.punchline: Annie is fully committed to the bit and has named her character 'Fibrosis' — a medical condition — delivered with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Annie fully committing to a name that sounds like a respiratory disease is funny precisely because she delivers it with total sincerity. The name choice implies she was going for something fantasy-sounding and landed on a medical term.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Well, structurally speaking, the bridge needed to collapse for the narrative arc. If it had held, we'd have no third act conflict, no character growth, and frankly, no reason for anyone to learn anything about themselves or each other. Plus, I may have based the calculations on a TV show where they do that thing where they always build it wrong the first time.

jokes.text: Hector the Well-Endowed? Again? / You think that's a weird coincidence? I'm a troll named Dingleberry. That's my mom's nickname for me.
jokes.setup: Characters are announcing D&D names; Jeff notes Chang has gotten 'Hector the Well-Endowed' again (as in the previous D&D episode).
jokes.punchline: Chang is unbothered — he pivots to Jeff's character name 'Dingleberry' and reveals it's his mother's nickname for him.
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: the callback to Chang getting the same character works as a running gag for rewatchers. But the stronger beat is Chang pivoting to 'Dingleberry... that's my mom's nickname for me' — it's bizarre and specific and implies a strange family dynamic. Classic Chang non sequitur with just enough detail to suggest a whole tragic backstory.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Nobody invited me to my grandson's birthday party. Can you believe that?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I mean, what kind of family doesn't invite their grandfather?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, have you considered that maybe... they just don't like you?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: What? That's ridiculous!

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I'm a very likeable guy.

jokes.text: I protect the blade of Diehard... a family sword whose power knows no equal. In our clan, the leader carries the hilt, his eldest heir, the blade, for we believe man's greatest weapon against evil is the bond... 'Is the bond between father and son.'
jokes.setup: Hank reads his character sheet aloud and gradually realizes the entire backstory has been written to force a father-son reconciliation metaphor.
jokes.punchline: He pauses when he reaches the thematic punchline, then finishes reading it in quotes — audibly distancing himself from the sentiment — while the room registers the manipulation.
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe moment. The sword metaphor being so on-the-nose that Hank audibly 'quote-marks' the punchline is a sharp structural joke about the group's ham-fisted therapeutic design.

jokes.text: I go to Tristram, and I'm laughing... and I pick him up, and I carry him to the bridge. It's fun.
jokes.setup: Jeff has said 'the only winner is fun' — now Hickey attempts to demonstrate fun by narrating that he's having it, while the forced quality undercuts everything.
jokes.punchline: Hickey's flat cop delivery of 'and I carry him to the bridge. It's fun.' — asserting fun as a fact in his usual monotone — is the comedic payoff.
jokes.explanation: Hickey narrating forced fun in his interrogation-room voice is a great character-integration joke. The structure — building to 'It's fun' as a terse declarative sentence — is perfect. Only a character like Hickey would categorically state his own enjoyment as if filing a report.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I propose a competition to see who can summon the most powerful necrophile.

jokes.text: I cast 'Torvin's Flesh of Fire.' / Tristram murmurs an incantation. His body becomes wreathed in white hot flame, burning Hector for... Six damage. / Hey!
jokes.setup: Hickey has picked up Chang's character (Hector) to force him to the bridge. Jeff's character retaliates by casting a fire spell on Hector.
jokes.punchline: The spell is genuine — Chang takes real damage — and his simple 'Hey!' is the perfect reaction to being set on fire for being carried.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation gag — Jeff retaliating against Hickey by burning Chang is petty and funny. Chang's 'Hey!' is the right one-word reaction. The game's internal logic being used for interpersonal spite is solid.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Listen up! You want to know what builds real teamwork? Fear. Primal, existential fear. So here's what's gonna happen - you're all gonna work together, or I'm gonna hurt you.

jokes.text: Hector, that's called self-defence.
jokes.setup: Chang objects to being set on fire.
jokes.punchline: Jeff claims setting someone on fire when they were being carried by a third party constitutes 'self-defence' — an absurd legal reasoning applied to D&D combat.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's straight-faced invocation of 'self-defence' for magically immolating someone is a good short joke. The legal framing applied to fantasy violence is a solid beat.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Tiny Nuggins scampers into the jungle.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not a scamper, that's a full combat crawl like the Viet Cong used in the Tet Offensive.

jokes.text: Abed, considering the bigger picture... you think it might be possible you miscalculated the bridge strength?
jokes.setup: Jeff's fire spell has set the bridge on fire, causing it to collapse, plunging everyone into a river.
jokes.punchline: Jeff, whose spell caused the disaster, is now passive-aggressively trying to shift blame to Abed the DM for 'miscalculating' bridge strength rather than acknowledging he set it on fire.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff deflection — the phrasing 'considering the bigger picture' as a prelude to avoiding responsibility is very Winger. The specific accusation that Abed 'miscalculated bridge strength' as if it's an engineering oversight (rather than Jeff setting it on fire) is a sharp irony.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Hobgoblins are a humanoid monster in fantasy settings, similar to orcs but generally more intelligent and organized.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: They're worth 15 Scrabble points.

jokes.text: Would've been constructed in the third age by goblins. They used primitive iron anchors.
jokes.setup: Jeff is implying Abed made a DM error by having the bridge collapse.
jokes.punchline: Abed counters with highly specific in-world lore — the bridge was structurally compromised from the outset due to goblin construction — delivered with total calm.
jokes.explanation: Abed's completely calm, forensically detailed explanation of why goblin bridge construction was substandard is funny because: (a) it implies he had this backstory ready, (b) it completely ignores Jeff's fire spell as the actual cause. His total lack of defensive irritation is perfect deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait! There are ladies present. Gentlemen first!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I shall protect your honor with my sword!

jokes.text: You plunge into the icy, raging waters of Skull River. / What? / You know, what's your problem? / What? / You didn't invite me to Sebastian's birthday.
jokes.setup: Everyone has fallen into the river; in-game chaos unfolds. Then Hickey and Hank suddenly break from the fiction to have their real argument.
jokes.punchline: The abrupt rupture from D&D narration to raw family confrontation — 'You didn't invite me to Sebastian's birthday' — is a tonal gear-shift that recontextualizes the whole scene.
jokes.explanation: Good structural moment — the multiple 'What?'s create a moment of comedic disorientation before the reveal of the real fight erupting through the game fiction. The intrusion of genuine family drama into the D&D framework is what the episode builds toward and this is its first major crack.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Hey hobgoblins! Yeah, you heard me! You're just goblins with a hobby!

jokes.text: They're not together. / Not helping! / Be a bad Dungeon Master if I was.
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a speech about fathers and sons being together. Abed points out they've literally been split into separate groups.
jokes.punchline: Jeff snaps 'Not helping!' and Abed replies with the perfectly calm, almost philosophically neutral 'Be a bad Dungeon Master if I was' — his commitment to the fiction over the therapy is total.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest Abed beats. His DM ethics trumping any therapeutic concern is perfect character comedy. 'Be a bad Dungeon Master if I was' is a great line — it has the laconic authority of a professional code of conduct. The inversion of expected helpfulness is sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I've loved you all so much. You've been like family to me. I want you to know that whatever happens, I'm at peace.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Shirley, we love you too. You've meant everything to us.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: But Jeff... why did you never return my Tupperware from 2010?

jokes.text: I didn't invite you to the birthday party because I wanted to enjoy it.
jokes.setup: Hank explains why he didn't invite his father to his son's birthday.
jokes.punchline: The blunt honesty of 'because I wanted to enjoy it' — no euphemism, no softening — lands as dark comedy precisely because of its directness.
jokes.explanation: Hank's brutal honesty is funny in its completeness — there's no meanness intended, just pure factual statement. The audience simultaneously laughs and winces. Good dark-subversive beat that reveals the genuine depth of the rift.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I've punched exactly 847 hearts in my life, and I've never missed once. That's a perfect record. I could punch a heart in a pitch-black room while riding a unicycle backwards during an earthquake, and I'd still hit it dead center.

jokes.text: If I kill the necrophile before you do, I come to my grandson's birthday.
jokes.setup: Hickey proposes a competition — whoever kills the necromancer first wins the right to attend the birthday.
jokes.punchline: He calls the necromancer a 'necrophile' — a malapropism that substitutes the game term with a word that means something very different and much darker.
jokes.explanation: Classic Hickey malapropism — 'necrophile' vs. 'necromancer' is a funny error because the wrong word is so much more alarming. It plays perfectly against his confident, authoritative delivery. The fact that no one corrects him in this moment adds to the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We should take a moment to honor their memory.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Now, who wants their stuff?

jokes.text: If I kill the necromancer before you do, then you don't go to Christmas or Thanksgiving at Aunt Rachel's. / You don't even go to that. / Yeah, but I will if you don't.
jokes.setup: The competition terms are being negotiated.
jokes.punchline: Hank's stakes are that Hickey won't come to Aunt Rachel's holiday dinners — Hickey points out he doesn't even go to those — and Hank's response ('Yeah, but I will if you don't') reveals he only wants to attend specifically to exclude his father.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant escalation. The reveal that Hank doesn't actually want to go to Aunt Rachel's but will specifically attend to prevent his father from going is a devastating character detail delivered as a punchline. It's both funny and genuinely revealing about the father-son relationship — the spite runs so deep that the goal isn't enjoyment but exclusion. Well-structured three-beat exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: A fair?

jokes.text: Well, I'm assuming you guys can help me beat him... because if we lose, I'm gonna punch each of you in the heart.
jokes.setup: Hickey has accepted Hank's challenge and now turns to recruit the study group as his allies.
jokes.punchline: His recruitment pitch ends with a threat: failure means he will literally punch them each in the heart.
jokes.explanation: Classic Hickey — his version of team motivation is a threat of cardiac violence. 'Punch each of you in the heart' is a specific, anatomically precise threat that becomes this episode's running motif. Only Hickey could make this his pep talk.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'll get the vacuum!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Time to spray some Raid!

jokes.text: I build a fire and construct a crude wooden rack to dry my boots and oversized codpiece.
jokes.setup: The group has washed up on a riverbank after falling in. Characters are narrating survival actions.
jokes.punchline: Dean Pelton narrates survival needs — and includes drying his 'oversized codpiece' as matter-of-factly as his boots.
jokes.explanation: Dean Pelton specifying the 'oversized' codpiece as a practical survival concern is a perfect character-integrated joke. His preoccupation with his own fantasy self-image manifesting in D&D is very Dean. The word 'oversized' doing a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Sky spiders aren't dangerous. They're actually beneficial to the ecosystem.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Unlike sky mosquitoes, which will literally kill you.

jokes.text: Build a fire? Horse s'mores? Screw this. The river runs east. I head west.
jokes.setup: The group is settling into campfire survival mode; Shirley's character Tiny Nuggins has had enough.
jokes.punchline: Shirley flatly dismisses the whole survival camp scenario ('Screw this') and immediately moves counter to the river's direction — west instead of east — suggesting Tiny Nuggins is both impatient and directionally contrarian.
jokes.explanation: Shirley breaking from group survival activities with 'Screw this' is funny in context because it's also a very Shirley-as-Tiny-Nuggins thief move: independent, practical, disruptive. The specificity of going west because east is where the river goes is a nicely absurd survival logic.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So, uh, nice weather we're having. For the apocalypse, I mean.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You guys come here often? To destroy civilization?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I gotta say, your exoskeletons are really... shiny. Very intimidating in a professional way.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So what's your deal? Are you more of a 'destroy humanity' spider or more of a 'live and let live' spider?

jokes.text: Hey, I didn't scamper in the jungles of Nicaragua and I won't do it now.
jokes.setup: Abed narrates that Tiny Nuggins 'scampers' into the jungle.
jokes.punchline: Shirley objects in character to the word 'scamper' — drawing on a Nicaragua backstory that is both funny as an unexpected detail and a Shirley character moment (she's dignified and doesn't scamper).
jokes.explanation: Excellent Shirley line. The Nicaragua reference implies a whole untold backstory (what was Shirley doing there?), and her specific objection to the indignity of 'scamper' — not the jungle, not the danger, but the word — is perfect character comedy. 'I didn't scamper in the jungles of Nicaragua' as a statement of personal code is quotable and memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Dude, these spider chicks are totally hot. I'm gonna tap that.

jokes.text: Tiny Nuggins, if we rest, we'll regain our strength. / And lose my family. / I'll imaginary sleep when I'm imaginary dead.
jokes.setup: Jeff's character suggests resting to recover. Shirley refuses, citing stakes.
jokes.punchline: 'I'll imaginary sleep when I'm imaginary dead' — a variation on 'I'll sleep when I'm dead' modified for the fiction, delivered as genuine determination.
jokes.explanation: Superb line. 'I'll imaginary sleep when I'm imaginary dead' is a perfect modification of a classic phrase that works on multiple levels: it's a sincere expression of Shirley's stakes, it acknowledges the fictional frame while operating within it, and it's beautifully economical. High quotability — this is the kind of line fans repeat. The double use of 'imaginary' is the key craft choice.

jokes.text: In Scrabble than regular goblins.
jokes.setup: Abed introduces 'hobgoblins' as enemies — larger and stronger than goblins.
jokes.punchline: He adds that they're worth more 'in Scrabble than regular goblins' — a completely irrelevant comparative metric that implies D&D creatures have been cross-referenced with Scrabble tile values.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Abed ranking hobgoblins vs. goblins using Scrabble tile values is an absurdist non sequitur delivered with total DM authority. It implies Abed has actually cross-referenced D&D monster manuals with Scrabble letter scores. The specificity makes it brilliant — not just 'they're harder' but a system of value derived from an entirely unrelated game. Perfect economy, originality, and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: He said you were getting fat.

dialogue.speaker: Goblin
dialogue.line: What? No, we were just talking about how much we appreciate each other's friendship.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: He also said your voice is annoying.

jokes.text: I punch him in the heart and I keep running.
jokes.setup: Shirley's Tiny Nuggins is charging recklessly at hobgoblins; someone urges caution.
jokes.punchline: Hickey narrates attacking by punching in the heart — establishing his signature combat move that callbacks his earlier threat to the group.
jokes.explanation: Good running gag seed — Hickey's heart-punching is now his combat signature. The callback to his earlier threat is satisfying, and 'I punch him in the heart and I keep running' has the cadence of a man filing an action report.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I may have suggested to Gerald that little Murg doesn't actually have his ears, and that perhaps he should look into that.

jokes.text: There are no women with them, are there? I got class.
jokes.setup: Hobgoblins are charging; Hickey is about to attack them.
jokes.punchline: Before attacking, Hickey checks if there are women present — not because he won't fight them, but as a matter of personal chivalry ('I got class').
jokes.explanation: Good Hickey character bit — the old-fashioned chivalry code being applied to fantasy combat is funny. 'I got class' as a self-assessment while preparing to fight monsters is a nicely absurd self-image moment.

jokes.text: Go find a name that's not just another creature's name plus 'hob.'
jokes.setup: Shirley has helped drive off the hobgoblins.
jokes.punchline: She trash-talks the retreating hobgoblins by pointing out that 'hobgoblin' is literally just 'goblin' with 'hob' tacked on — a pointed critique of D&D naming conventions delivered as genuine insult.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Shirley trash-talking retreating fantasy monsters by critiquing their naming convention is unexpected and sharp. The observation is actually linguistically accurate (hobgoblin = hob + goblin) which makes it land as genuine wit rather than just absurdism. 'Go find a name that's not just another creature's name plus hob' is highly quotable and shows Shirley-as-Tiny-Nuggins has genuine game-world confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: When you rub a sword, you're not just maintaining steel. You're connecting with something magical, something primal. The friction, the pressure, the rhythmic motion—it builds between you and the blade until you both glisten with—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, Hank, we got it.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: —and the release when you finally finish. Pure. Transcendent.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's enough sword talk.

jokes.text: She was badly wounded from her fall in the Skull River... and the arrows were just too much. I'm sorry. / That's it? Is she dead? / Yes, that's it, Hickey.
jokes.setup: Annie's character Crouton has been badly wounded during the hobgoblin fight.
jokes.punchline: Abed's clinical, apologetic death announcement — 'the arrows were just too much. I'm sorry.' — is delivered with the flat affect of a DM who has absolutely no emotional stakes in this.
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan Abed DM moment. The clinical 'I'm sorry' after 'the arrows were just too much' is funny in its lack of dramatic weight. Hickey's 'That's it?' has the genuine incredulity of a player who just lost a character unexpectedly.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Before we do this, I need to know—who ate all the popcorn from the study room? Because I specifically labeled that bag with my name, and now it's gone, and I'm genuinely upset about it.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Okay, anyway, back to this whole impending conflict situation. Let's do this.

jokes.text: I'm dead. But it's okay. I'm on your side. Which is why I'm dead. And I may be gone... but just remember whenever the wind whispers through the woods... you got me killed.
jokes.setup: Crouton (Annie) has just been killed. She offers final words.
jokes.punchline: Annie builds toward what sounds like a sincere, touching farewell speech — then pivots to 'you got me killed' as her parting wisdom.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is exquisite — Annie performs the full arc of a 'dying companion speech' complete with the poetic 'whenever the wind whispers through the woods' flourish, then lands on the bluntest possible punchline: 'you got me killed.' The setup earns its ironic subversion completely. It's funny, it's sharp, and it has great Annie character integration (she's both sincere and passive-aggressively pointed). Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: You know what? I don't care about winning. But Hank? Hank cares too much. It's unhealthy. The man's obsessed.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Unlike me. I'm perfectly balanced. I don't need to win at anything.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Except I've won 47 consecutive Paintball competitions. I have a trophy room. I've alphabetized my trophies by event name, then by year, then by opponent defeated.

jokes.text: Now, you listen to me, young man. I've punched about a thousand hearts in my life. I never, never missed. / You ever been a 3-foot tall halfling running through 2-foot high vines trying to punch a 7-foot monster?
jokes.setup: Hickey reprimands Hank for missing his heart-punch attack on a hobgoblin.
jokes.punchline: Hank perfectly skewers the physics of his father's bravado — Hickey may have punched a thousand hearts, but those hearts weren't attached to 7-foot monsters while he was 3 feet tall.
jokes.explanation: Great escalation of the heart-punching gag. Hank's rebuttal is precisely specific — the exact height differential, the vine obstacle, the monster height — making a logical counter-argument to his father's machismo using the game's own internal physics. The specificity is what makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: You see, the way I figure it, keeping a man from his family is a fundamental rights issue. It's right up there with freedom of speech and the right to bear arms. So when that necromancer tried to keep me from seeing my boy, well, that's when I knew I had to take him down.

jokes.text: I take a moment of silence to mourn my fallen comrade, Crouton... before rifling through her belongings.
jokes.setup: Crouton (Annie) has just died. The group is processing the loss.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's Tiny Nuggins observes a moment of silence — then immediately loots the corpse. The pause before 'before rifling through her belongings' is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: Superb structural joke. The first clause performs sincere mourning — Shirley gives it full dignity — and the second clause instantly undercuts it with the thiefly practicality of looting a friend's corpse. 'Before rifling through her belongings' is a beautiful phrase. The structure (solemn comma, pivot) is textbook comedic economy. Perfect for Shirley's thief character: dignified and mercenary simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Dad, I just want to—

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: WHAT ARE YOU DOING?! Is this an attack?!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, I'm trying to hug you—

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: A HUG?! That's what they WANT us to think! Diversionary tactic!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Dad, please—

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: I'm going in! HYAH!

jokes.text: But you know where he was for most of my birthdays? Little place that rhymes with 'not there.' / Times Square?
jokes.setup: Hank is explaining the depth of his resentment toward his father.
jokes.punchline: He uses the classic 'rhymes with...' setup for 'not there' — but Jeff's immediate answer is the wrong literal rhyme ('Times Square'), deflating the emotional beat with idiocy.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: Hank deploys a sincere emotional device ('little place that rhymes with not there'), it sets up a moment of pathos — then Jeff's completely wrong-headed answer 'Times Square' punctures the solemnity with pure stupidity. The timing depends on Jeff answering instantly and confidently. High quotability, strong structure, and the callback is both funny and a good Jeff character moment (he disrupts emotional sincerity reflexively).

jokes.text: I draw my sword, and I cry out, 'Back, eight-legged demons! I will not scoop you up with a catalogue and let you outside on this day!'
jokes.setup: Three huge winged arachnids — 'Sky Spiders' — appear. The group must decide how to respond.
jokes.punchline: Hank's battle cry is a spider-removal technique from domestic life — using a catalogue to scoop spiders outside — applied to giant fantasy monsters.
jokes.explanation: Excellent, original joke. The specificity of 'with a catalogue' as the medium of spider relocation makes it brilliant — not just 'let outside' but the precise domestic technique. The fact that Hank threatens the Sky Spiders with the promise of NOT scooping them with a catalogue is a funny logical inversion. It also inadvertently humanizes Hank (he's a gentle person at home). Very quotable, highly original.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're all missing the point. The ending isn't anticlimactic—it's narratively honest. Not every story needs a explosive finale. Sometimes the most satisfying conclusion is the one that respects internal logic and character development over spectacle. That's actually more sophisticated storytelling.

jokes.text: I cast 'Speak with Monsters,' and I say: 'Hello. You're looking well.'
jokes.setup: Hank has drawn his sword against the Sky Spiders; Tristram intercepts.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's opening diplomatic gambit with a giant monster is the most anodyne social pleasantry imaginable: 'Hello. You're looking well.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — Jeff casts a spell that unlocks monster communication, and his opener is a banal social pleasantry. 'You're looking well' said to an enormous hairy arachnid is funny precisely because it's the least frightening possible first contact. Good Jeff character integration: he's fundamentally a smooth-talker who defaults to social charm.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I am the Dungeon Master. I decide what happens in this world. You don't get to demand endings. You play by my rules, or you don't play at all. I am a god in this world, and gods don't negotiate with mortals.

jokes.text: The lead spider bends four knees and twitches its hairy ovipositor... rhythmically secreting and retracting a giant droplet... Or drop... of silk.
jokes.setup: The Sky Spider is responding to Jeff's diplomatic greeting with a physical display.
jokes.punchline: Abed describes the arachnid's 'hairy ovipositor rhythmically secreting and retracting a giant droplet' — narrating this with technical DM precision before mildly course-correcting ('Or drop... of silk').
jokes.explanation: Abed describing something that sounds progressively more sexually suggestive before flatly clarifying 'of silk' is good cringe comedy. The brief pause and 'Or drop...' mid-sentence implies even Abed noticed the trajectory of his own narration.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Even in the afterlife, you need to eat a balanced breakfast. I've got some casserole in the oven upstairs.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: And don't forget to call your mother, honey. Oh wait, you can now. I'm right here.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Most importantly, always wear clean underwear. You never know when you'll end up in heaven or the hospital.

jokes.text: Damn, you made that Sky Spider your bitch, yo!
jokes.setup: Jeff has successfully communicated with and appeased the Sky Spider.
jokes.punchline: Dean Pelton's celebration of Jeff's diplomatic success in street vernacular — including 'yo' — is an absurd tonal collision for a Dean character who has been in a fantasy role-play.
jokes.explanation: Decent Dean moment — the contrast between the high-fantasy setting and his sudden street vernacular is reliable Dean comedy. The enthusiasm is characterful but the joke itself is fairly standard register-contrast humor.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, so Hickey and Hank are actually... getting along?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: They found their thing. D&D.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: But they hate each other.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Exactly. It's the perfect dysfunctional compromise. They get to complain about the game instead of each other.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's actually beautiful. They've weaponized escapism.

jokes.text: One guard hob-guards. What they call guarding.
jokes.setup: The other group has tracked hobgoblins to a shack with a guard outside.
jokes.punchline: Abed clarifies the hobgoblin is 'hob-guarding' — implying the verb form of their species name is their job title, delivered as dry D&D lore.
jokes.explanation: Abed's dry parenthetical — 'What they call guarding' — applied to creating 'hob-guard' as a verb is a great DM voice joke. It callbacks the earlier 'just another creature's name plus hob' observation and implies the hobgoblin world is entirely constructed around the prefix.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: They're like a couple that can't break up because they have a kid together. Except the kid is their entire relationship.

jokes.text: Drop on the last one and grapple. / You got a hold of him. / This one is for Crouton.
jokes.setup: The group is clearing the hobgoblin shack efficiently.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's declaration 'This one is for Crouton' — invoking the name of the friend she looted immediately after mourning — as battle-cry is a great dark callback.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that plays on the absurdity of Shirley immediately looting Crouton's body. 'This one is for Crouton' as vengeance is funnier knowing Shirley rifled through her stuff two scenes ago. The sincerity of the battle dedication elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm done. Everyone's dead. The game is over.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: But Abed, we were just getting to the best part!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No. Nuclear explosion. Everyone dies. Including you, Dean.

jokes.text: Hi. I'm Tiny Nuggins. I'm gonna put my dagger down right here, so we can just talk.
jokes.setup: Two hobgoblins have been captured; the group wants information about the necromancer.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's character Tiny Nuggins — who just slaughtered goblins while yelling 'This one is for Crouton' — now puts on a good-cop persona with a dagger-down opening gambit.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the interrogation sequence. Shirley's immediate pivot from warrior to soft-voiced negotiator is funny, particularly since she still has goblin blood on her (presumably).

jokes.text: Human trash. / Yeah, look, I'm gonna give it to you straight. We're looking for a necromancer. We don't need two goblins to find him. So between you and your friend, who do you think's the most useful?
jokes.setup: Shirley is interrogating a captured goblin diplomatically.
jokes.punchline: Despite the goblin calling her 'human trash,' Shirley calmly pivots to a 'we don't need both of you alive' negotiation tactic.
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy — Shirley's calm response to being called 'human trash' by pivoting to implied execution of the less useful goblin is a funny tonal shift. The good-cop-becomes-bad-cop-immediately is sharp.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah, because of that famous goblin loyalty. I could never drive a wedge between you and some guy from work. / I was best man at that guy's wedding.
jokes.setup: One goblin refuses to betray the other. Shirley sarcastically references 'goblin loyalty.'
jokes.punchline: The goblin counters with genuine indignation: 'I was best man at that guy's wedding' — the hobgoblin has real, human-scale social bonds.
jokes.explanation: Good subversion — the joke assumes goblins have no real social bonds, then the goblin asserts a specific, socially significant one (best man at a wedding). It makes the goblins more sympathetically funny while also making Shirley's interrogation tactics more morally interesting. The specificity of 'best man' as opposed to just 'friend' adds pathos-comedy.

jokes.text: Your friend says you just got married. Congratulations. Too bad about the food.
jokes.setup: Shirley begins fabricating information the other goblin 'said' to drive a wedge.
jokes.punchline: 'Congratulations. Too bad about the food.' — Shirley commiserates about the wedding food quality as a manipulation tactic, implying the other goblin complained about the reception.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. 'Too bad about the food' is a beautiful interrogation wedge — it's simultaneously an absurd detail (Shirley is making up goblin wedding catering complaints) and a perfect deployment of Shirley's character (she cares deeply about hospitality and would know exactly how to weaponize catering criticism). The goblin's reaction ('What about the food?') shows it worked instantly. Great structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Oh, I guess he didn't like your wedding toast. / Golbak said that? / Klang doesn't approve of you and Lisa, Golbak... and I don't get the sense it's because of his feelings for you.
jokes.setup: The wedding food wedge has worked; Shirley escalates by inventing a critical wedding toast.
jokes.punchline: She keeps escalating: not just food, now Klang doesn't approve of Golbak's marriage — and 'I don't get the sense it's because of his feelings for you' implies Klang is in love with Lisa, not Golbak.
jokes.explanation: The goblin-relationship drama is surprisingly well-constructed as a micro-plot. The implication that Klang is in love with Lisa (Golbak's new wife) is a genuinely clever escalation. Shirley's interrogation skills are both funny and competent — she's very good at this, which is a character revelation.

jokes.text: I think about Lisa, sitting in that hole in Darktooth Canyon... with that little Frimrok and Grignog rolling about on the wolf pelts. Come on, between you and me, which one do you think is yours?
jokes.setup: Shirley is pushing deeper into the fabricated goblin drama to break Golbak's loyalty.
jokes.punchline: She invents names for Lisa's children (Frimrok and Grignog), places them in a specific location, and implies paternity doubt — 'which one do you think is yours?' — with the calm of someone who absolutely knows what she's doing.
jokes.explanation: Peak of the goblin interrogation sequence. The names 'Frimrok and Grignog' are perfectly absurd D&D-ish goblin-child names. The 'rolling about on the wolf pelts' detail is a great environmental specificity. And 'which one do you think is yours?' as the culminating question is a beautiful, devastating escalation. Shirley as master manipulator using paternity doubt on a fantasy goblin is both hilarious and oddly humanizing of the goblins.

jokes.text: Father, forgive me. I have travelled so far from you. How many game days since the Skull River ripped us apart? How many real hours since I've gone pee?
jokes.setup: Hank's character is delivering a sincere, poetic monologue about being separated from his father.
jokes.punchline: Buried in the poetic speech about distance is 'How many real hours since I've gone pee?' — shattering the fiction by noting a physical need in the middle of a letter to his fictional father.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke. The setup is a sincere (if grandiose) speech about separation; the punchline ruptures it with a mundane bodily need that intrudes on the fiction. The parallel structure ('how many game days... how many real hours') makes the pee reference land perfectly — it mimics the cadence of the poetic line before subverting it. High marks for structure and economy.

jokes.text: According to my character sheet... if I rub the blade of our magic family sword while you rub the hilt... twin beacons of light will reveal our locations to each other. Each night, I will think of you and rub... praying for the night fate will find us rubbing together.
jokes.setup: Hank is reading his character's sword mechanics to try to reunite with the other group.
jokes.punchline: The mechanics of the father-son sword (rubbing hilt and blade) become progressively more sexually suggestive as Hank reads them aloud, culminating in 'rubbing together.'
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe joke about the unintentional double entendre of sword-rubbing mechanics written as a father-son bonding device. Hank's earnest delivery makes it funnier — he's apparently not catching it. The escalation from 'rub' to 'rubbing together' is well-paced.

jokes.text: 'Abed, I rub my sword's hilt'? / Beam of light shoots up from your location as the hilt of Diehard seeks its blade.
jokes.setup: A sparrow arrives with Hank's note; Hickey reads it aloud.
jokes.punchline: The note asks Hickey to rub his sword's hilt. Hickey reads this with the flat skepticism of a man deeply unsure about these instructions. Abed remains completely unrattled.
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat — Hickey's incredulous reading of the note followed by Abed's immediate clinical response ignoring any potential awkwardness. Hickey's visible discomfort with the instructions he doesn't question is a good character moment.

jokes.text: Does anybody have a toothpick? I got a piece of popcorn stuck in my tooth. Like, right under the gum. I've been trying like for 15 minutes... with, you know, my tooth and then with my tongue and my finger.
jokes.setup: An intensely dramatic moment — both groups converging on the tower, possibly going to war — Abed intones 'this may end in war.'
jokes.punchline: Hickey immediately interrupts the dramatic narration to ask for a toothpick, describing his popcorn-tooth situation in granular detail.
jokes.explanation: Perfect tonal subversion. The epic narration is interrupted by one of the most mundane bodily complaints imaginable, and Hickey's level of detail — 'with my tooth and then with my tongue and my finger' — makes it funnier. The specificity of his failed attempts (tried three different tools, in order) is very Hickey: methodical even in triviality. The DM moment deflation is a classic Community bit.

jokes.text: Oh, hello, there we go. Anyway... But it may end in war.
jokes.setup: Hickey has been distracted mid-epic-moment by the popcorn in his tooth.
jokes.punchline: He dislodges it with a satisfied 'Oh, hello, there we go' — then Abed picks up exactly where he left off with 'But it may end in war' — as if none of that happened.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. Abed resuming with 'But it may end in war' at exactly the right moment — after the satisfied dental resolution — is excellent comic timing. The two characters' complete tonal divergence (mundane/epic) and Abed's refusal to acknowledge the interruption is very good.

jokes.text: You've seen the way he talks to me, doesn't want his father in his life. He'll do anything to win... This is a man who thinks of grandchildren like trophies.
jokes.setup: Hickey is trying to convince Dean Pelton's group to fight against Hank.
jokes.punchline: Hickey characterizes his son as a monster — 'thinks of grandchildren like trophies' — while himself treating access to his grandson as a D&D competition prize.
jokes.explanation: Good irony — Hickey accuses Hank of treating grandchildren like trophies while he himself proposed a contest where the prize is access to the grandchild. The lack of self-awareness is perfectly Hickey, and the ironic framing is clear to the audience.

jokes.text: Rise, brave, sweet Dingleberry. Rise.
jokes.setup: Hickey is rallying his fallen troops (Chang's character) before the final confrontation.
jokes.punchline: His solemn battle speech is addressed to 'Dingleberry' — Chang's character, whose name also happens to be Hickey's mother's nickname for Jeff.
jokes.explanation: Good callback — the gravity of 'Rise, brave, sweet...' applied to 'Dingleberry' is an inherently funny tonal collision, and it callbacks the name reveal from earlier. The word 'sweet' before the name is especially good.

jokes.text: We are here so Tristram Steelheart, Lord of the Sky Spiders, can slay the necromancer.
jokes.setup: Jeff's character greets Hank's group at the tower.
jokes.punchline: Jeff has promoted himself — his character is now 'Lord of the Sky Spiders' — a title he gave himself based on the earlier sky spider diplomacy.
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff — Jeff's sky spider parlaying has become a title. His appropriation of an improvised title reveals his character's ego. 'Lord of the Sky Spiders' is an impressive and specific D&D title that Jeff apparently awarded himself.

jokes.text: Tiny Nuggins, Waterboarder of Goblins, will do the slaying... because every man has the right to hang out with his grandson.
jokes.setup: Jeff has claimed the right to kill the necromancer for Hickey's team.
jokes.punchline: Shirley counters by declaring her title — 'Waterboarder of Goblins' — which is a callback to her interrogation while also being a horrifying description that she delivers with cheerful sincerity.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and most quotable lines. 'Tiny Nuggins, Waterboarder of Goblins' perfectly synthesizes Shirley's interrogation sequence into a self-awarded title. The fact that she uses 'waterboarder' — referencing a real and controversial interrogation technique — applied to fantasy goblins, delivered by Shirley with complete moral authority, is brilliantly dark. High originality, great character integration, perfectly economical. This rivals the other top jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: No, they're not. / I'm not part of this. I am Joseph Gordon Diehard... and I am only here to hug my father, which I now do.
jokes.setup: Hickey says they're not outnumbered; Dean says they are. Tension builds for a D&D battle.
jokes.punchline: Hank completely defects from the competition — breaking with his team and his own competitive stance — and simply declares he is here to hug his father.
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of the expected battle escalation. Hank resolving the situation through a sincere emotional gesture is funny because it's so out of proportion with all the competitive buildup, and because it throws everyone's plans into chaos. 'Which I now do' as a declaration before hugging is a great character-maintaining quirk.

jokes.text: I am Joseph Gordon Diehard... and I am only here to hug my father, which I now do.
jokes.setup: Hank defects from his team to reunite with Hickey
jokes.punchline: 'Which I now do' — the most deadpan possible way to describe performing an emotional act. The simultaneity of the declaration and execution ('I now do') is funny in its procedural flatness.
jokes.explanation: The procedural 'which I now do' applied to a hug is very funny — it's the D&D action-declaration format applied to emotional reunion. Keeps the scene from being too sentimental. Good economy.

jokes.text: It's a trick! / I'm not letting him hug me. / I hug my father! / He has gunpowder in his pants.
jokes.setup: Hank attempts a sincere hug of his father; Hickey's team interprets it as a tactical move.
jokes.punchline: Chang's accusation that Hank 'has gunpowder in his pants' is an absurd escalation that makes no sense in D&D terms but perfectly captures the paranoid atmosphere.
jokes.explanation: Good chaos beat. The escalating misreading of a sincere hug as a military action — culminating in the specific accusation of trouser-gunpowder — is funny absurdism. Chang's contribution is reliably bizarre.

jokes.text: You're impaled. / Worth it.
jokes.setup: Total chaos has erupted — everyone is fighting. Hank keeps pushing forward to hug his father despite combat.
jokes.punchline: He gets impaled. His response: 'Worth it.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word punchline. 'Worth it' is maximally economical — two syllables that complete the arc of Hank's entire character journey in this episode. His willingness to take a D&D impalement to hug his father is both a game-logic joke and a genuine emotional beat. The structure (impalement announced, beat, 'Worth it') is textbook. Among the episode's most quotable moments.

jokes.text: Son slayer! / I attack Jeff! / Arrow at Chang! / Arrow at Annie! / I head for the door. / Taste the blade of Diehard! / Lightning bolt, lightning bolt! / I spray all over them. / I hold Britta's face in a puddle. / Dingleberry smash! / After that, I put one right behind the ear.
jokes.setup: The impalement of Hank triggers a free-for-all battle where both groups attack each other.
jokes.punchline: The chaotic battle narration becomes a cascade of absurd D&D actions delivered at increasing speed — culminating in Hickey stating 'After that, I put one right behind the ear' with a hitman's calm.
jokes.explanation: The battle chaos is funny as a gestalt — the editing rhythm and escalating absurdity work visually and tonally. 'I spray all over them,' 'I hold Britta's face in a puddle,' and especially 'I put one right behind the ear' (execution-style) are the highlights. The sequence functions as comedic escalation rather than any single great joke.

jokes.text: Lightning bolt, lightning bolt! / Heal our moderate wounds! / I spray all over them. / I hold Britta's face in a puddle.
jokes.setup: An all-out D&D battle has erupted between the two teams — a free-for-all of spell-casting and attacks.
jokes.punchline: The rapid-fire action declarations escalate from heroic ('Lightning bolt!') through healing to 'I spray all over them' (vague and alarming) to 'I hold Britta's face in a puddle' — which is jarringly specific violence.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the battle declarations is well-structured, with 'I hold Britta's face in a puddle' as a specifically funny singling-out of Britta for targeted water violence. The escalation rhythm is good.

jokes.text: Top floor, one door. / I open it. / 'Flame Strike.' / You did already. / Mace! / Okay. Missed. / Hit him with a throwing dagger. / Used all your knives.
jokes.setup: Hickey and Shirley are the last survivors, pressing on to find the necromancer.
jokes.punchline: Every combat option Hickey tries, Abed blocks with a reason it won't work — she's out of knives, the spell was used, the mace missed — the systematic denial of all options is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good rapid-fire beat. The rhythm of Hickey proposing options and Abed systematically shutting them down is a nice DM-player dynamic. The comedic effect is cumulative — each denial adds to the mounting frustration comedy.

jokes.text: You see his bed, bottles of goop, some necromancing crap... but no necromancer.
jokes.setup: They've finally reached the necromancer's workshop after surviving everything.
jokes.punchline: Abed describes the lair in his characteristic flat inventory style — 'bottles of goop, some necromancing crap' — the last category being both dismissive and funny.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed DM flat description. 'Bottles of goop' and 'some necromancing crap' as inventory items are perfect — the second item especially, where 'crap' replaces any specific lore term. Only Abed could switch between hyper-specific world-building (goblin bridge construction, third age) and 'crap' in the same session.

jokes.text: Hey, I am a thief, not a wuss. I search too.
jokes.setup: Hickey asks if he can search the room, apparently worrying Shirley might backstab him.
jokes.punchline: Shirley, offended by the implication, clarifies that she's a thief (a D&D class) but that doesn't mean she's a wuss — the professional identity and personal pride are hilariously conflated.
jokes.explanation: Good Shirley line. 'I am a thief, not a wuss' treats the D&D class as a profession with its own dignity, and her insistence on searching alongside Hickey is funny given the professional tension. The straightforward delivery makes it land.

jokes.text: Hey, you can't just say he's gone. You owe us an ending. / I owe you nothing. I am a Dungeon Master. I create a boundless world, and I bind it by rules. Too heavy for a bridge? It breaks. Get hit? Take damage. Spend an hour outside someone's front door fighting over who gets to kill him? He leaves through the back.
jokes.setup: The necromancer has escaped through a back door. Hickey is furious that the DM let this happen.
jokes.punchline: Abed's declaration of DM authority is a perfectly structured speech that doubles as a critique of the group's behavior, delivered with the icy calm of someone who has been waiting to say this.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most memorable speeches. Abed's DM manifesto — 'I create a boundless world, and I bind it by rules' — is both a perfect character moment and an elegant summary of the episode's themes. The rule-examples are structured in ascending order of relevance: abstract physics rule, combat rule, then the specific accusation that their fighting caused the necromancer to escape. The speech is funny AND thematically perfect. High craft on structure and character integration — this is exclusively an Abed speech.

jokes.text: Hey, guys. Take it from a bunch of ghosts. This is no kind of life. You need fresh air and frozen yogurt. It's on me. Hug it out.
jokes.setup: Following Abed's DM speech, Annie's ghost character chimes in.
jokes.punchline: Annie, as a dead character speaking from beyond, dispenses life advice about fresh air and frozen yogurt — the mundane resolution offered from an ethereal state is funny.
jokes.explanation: Good Annie moment — the contrast between spectral authority ('take it from a bunch of ghosts') and the solution being frozen yogurt is funny. 'It's on me' as a ghost offering to pay is absurd. Decent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Gag me. / Who even uses that phrase?
jokes.setup: Annie says 'hug it out'; Hickey responds with 'gag me.'
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately calls out 'Gag me' as an outdated expression — both characters rejecting sentimentality in their own ways.
jokes.explanation: Quick, functional joke. Father and son inadvertently demonstrating their shared sarcasm by rejecting sentimentality in rapid succession is a decent character beat. 'Who even uses that phrase?' is a good burn on Hickey's dated slang.

jokes.text: I'm climbing down the ladder. I'm gonna find this guy. / I stay and search the workshop. / Any stuff there that can heal me? / Some potions. / Okay, well, I get half of that. / You just went down the ladder.
jokes.setup: Despite the emotional resolution moment, Hickey immediately resumes competitive game play.
jokes.punchline: He tries to claim potions from the workshop after declaring he went down the ladder — Abed catches the logical impossibility.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Hickey's refusal to let sentimentality interrupt his loot-gathering is very Hickey. The immediate return to game-tactical thinking undercuts any emotional progress nicely.

jokes.text: Okay, but I decide who gets what. / Fine, but we've gotta be wary of traps. / Wand of Orcus.
jokes.setup: Hickey and Shirley are negotiating loot division while trying to find the necromancer.
jokes.punchline: Their bickering descends into competing priorities — traps vs. wand cataloguing — until Hickey interrupts to announce 'Wand of Orcus' mid-negotiation.
jokes.explanation: Decent bit — the descent into loot-negotiation logistics as the ostensible emotional resolution continues to be undermined is a running theme. 'Wand of Orcus' as a mid-argument item callout is a good D&D-specific absurdist detail.

jokes.text: Do they like each other now? / Are you kidding me? They can't stand being in the same room. / I also don't think they can handle being apart. / And I think they just found a way to avoid doing either.
jokes.setup: Jeff watches Hickey and Shirley bickering about loot and traps as the episode's 'resolution.'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's analysis — they can't stand being together OR apart, so they found a way to avoid both — is delivered as both comedy and genuine insight.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best thematic observations. Jeff's three-beat analysis — can't stand together, can't handle apart, found a third option (the game) — is sharp writing that works as both a joke and the episode's thesis. It's a good Jeff moment because he's genuinely perceptive here. The rhythm of the three clauses is well-constructed.

jokes.text: And that's the best most fathers and sons can do.
jokes.setup: Jeff has identified the compromise Hickey and his son found.
jokes.punchline: Hank's dry addendum — 'that's the best most fathers and sons can do' — punctuates the observation with resigned wisdom delivered completely without self-pity.
jokes.explanation: Good final thematic button. The line is both funny and genuinely poignant. Hank's resignation is funny because it's delivered so matter-of-factly, but it also genuinely moves the needle emotionally. Good economy.

jokes.text: You've made me so proud today. / Know where we can buy a real sword? / Oh, Jeffrey.
jokes.setup: Hickey expresses pride in Jeff. It seems like a touching moment.
jokes.punchline: Jeff immediately asks where to buy a real sword — revealing the game has had a genuine effect on him — and Hickey's 'Oh, Jeffrey' is warmly exasperated, almost fatherly.
jokes.explanation: Good character-based ending beat. Jeff's immediate desire to buy a real sword after the game is a funny revelation of how thoroughly he got sucked in despite his skepticism throughout. And 'Oh, Jeffrey' — Hickey using Jeff's full name with warmth — is a lovely character moment. The joke works emotionally and comedically.

jokes.text: You're still at the entrance to the Chamber of Grief. Your move, Mr. Tickles.
jokes.setup: Post-credits tag: a completely new scene with Abed as DM for a new, unseen player.
jokes.punchline: Abed is running a D&D session for what appears to be a child or someone with an absurd character name 'Mr. Tickles' — the reveal is that Abed is always DMing.
jokes.explanation: Good tag. 'Mr. Tickles' as a D&D character name is funny, and 'Chamber of Grief' is a great dungeon name. Abed continuing to DM after everything implies this is simply what he does — a good character-based button. The unseen player adds intrigue.

jokes.text: You successfully pour more tea into Count Frogula's cup. That puts it at Hillary Rodham Kitten. Okay, you attempt to pass crumpets. You fail.
jokes.setup: Abed continues his tag scene — it becomes clear Mr. Tickles is playing tea party D&D.
jokes.punchline: Abed is applying full DM gravity to a child's tea party — tracking teacup fill levels and rolling for crumpet-passing — including a failure on the crumpet roll.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments and a perfect button for the episode. Abed applying D&D mechanics to a tea party — tracking liquid levels by named character ('Hillary Rodham Kitten'), rolling dice for crumpet success — is brilliantly absurd character comedy. The name 'Hillary Rodham Kitten' (riffing on Hillary Rodham Clinton) is unexpected and genuinely funny. 'You fail' on the crumpet pass is a perfect deadpan DM declaration. This is exclusively possible with Abed's character — his refusal to treat any game as beneath the gravity of his DM role. High craft, high impact.

jokes.text: I'm getting frustrated. If you take a look at your inventories, you'll see... Abed, are you almost done? / I can't sleep without my stuffies.
jokes.setup: Abed is managing an apparently difficult tea-party-D&D player who is getting frustrated with crumpet mechanics.
jokes.punchline: The scene is interrupted by someone (probably a parent or roommate) asking if Abed is almost done — revealing he has been keeping someone from their bedroom — and Abed's player announces 'I can't sleep without my stuffies,' confirming this is a very young child.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the tag. 'I can't sleep without my stuffies' confirms the player is a child, adding to the absurdity of Abed running a formal D&D session for a toddler. The parent/roommate interruption adds real-world stakes comedy.

jokes.text: Oh, a goblin notices you and murders you all. You're dead. They're all yours.
jokes.setup: Interrupted by an adult asking if he's done, Abed needs to end the tea-party session.
jokes.punchline: Abed dispenses with the entire tea-party game by instantly having a goblin kill all the characters — 'Oh, a goblin notices you and murders you all. You're dead.' — with zero ceremony, then immediately hands the stuffed animals to the parent.
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing joke. Abed's ruthless efficiency in ending the game — a goblin simply 'notices' and murders everyone, delivered with the same flat DM voice as his entire performance — is a beautiful character button. 'They're all yours' as he hands over the stuffed animals is a perfect final line. The joke works on multiple levels: it's a callback to his DM speech about rules (the goblin encounter is a valid game event), it's dark comedy (child characters summarily executed), and it's the perfect final Abed note. Very high craft — almost every element is working.

tmdb_overview: To help Hickey be a more involved grandfather, which means patching up a bad relationship with his son, the gang creates an epic role-playing game.
insight: D&D lore callbacks sustain a niche episode that peaks on character escalation rather than broad laughs.
